Issue:
Change in behaviour when saving a model instance with an explcit pk value if the pk field has a default
Description
	 
		(last modified by Reupen Shah)
	 
Consider the following model:
from uuid import uuid4
from django.db import models
class Sample(models.Model):
	id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid4)
	name = models.CharField(blank=True, max_length=100)
In Django 2.2 and earlier, the following commands would result in an INSERT followed by an UPDATE:
s0 = Sample.objects.create()
s1 = Sample(pk=s0.pk, name='Test 1')
s1.save()
However, in Django 3.0, this results in two INSERTs (naturally the second one fails). The behaviour also changes if default=uuid4 is removed from the id field.
This seems related to https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/29260.
The change in behaviour also has the side effect of changing the behaviour of the loaddata management command when the fixture contains explicit pk values and the objects already exist (e.g. when loading the fixture multiple times).
Perhaps the intention was to only change the behaviour if an explicit pk value was not set on the model instance being saved? (At least, that would be more backwards-compatible behaviour...)

django/db/models/base.py

The issue described is a change in behavior when saving a model instance with an explicit primary key (PK) value if the PK field has a default. In Django 2.2 and earlier, the following commands would result in an INSERT followed by an UPDATE:

```python
s0 = Sample.objects.create()
s1 = Sample(pk=s0.pk, name='Test 1')
s1.save()
```

However, in Django 3.0, this results in two INSERTs, which naturally causes the second INSERT to fail due to a unique constraint violation. The behavior also changes if `default=uuid4` is removed from the `id` field.

### Root Cause

The root cause of this issue is found in the `_save_table` method of `django/db/models/base.py`. Specifically, the condition that skips an UPDATE when adding an instance and the primary key has a default value:

```python
if (
    not force_insert and
    self._state.adding and
    self._meta.pk.default and
    self._meta.pk.default is not NOT_PROVIDED
):
    force_insert = True
```

This condition ensures that if the primary key has a default value and the instance is being added (i.e., not updated), an INSERT will be performed instead of an UPDATE. This change in behavior affects the `loaddata` management command when fixtures contain explicit PK values, causing it to fail if the objects already exist.

### Incorrect Behavior

In Django 3.0, the code forces an INSERT when the primary key has a default value, even if the primary key is explicitly set. This leads to a unique constraint violation when trying to insert a duplicate primary key.

### Expected Behavior

The expected behavior is that if an explicit primary key value is provided, an UPDATE should be performed instead of an INSERT, regardless of whether the primary key has a default value. This would maintain backward compatibility and prevent the unique constraint violation.

    self._meta.pk.default and
    self._meta.pk.default is not NOT_PROVIDED and
    not self._meta.pk.has_default_value(self)
):
    force_insert = True
